#### **Introduction** 

- **A** **_key feature of the precious met

als sector in June was the widespread reduction of Comex and Nymex investors positions as overbought conditions were unwound. Economic concerns also put pressure on silver and PGM prices. The speculative overhang in these metals is now much reduced, which takes away some overhead price resistance, but caution persists._** - **G** **_old dropped particularly sharply in late June as the Fed signalled no “QE3” and the IEA released oil reserves. An unsettled market is responding jumpily to external changes and remains vulnerable in the short term; $1,500 is important._** - **S** **_ilver’s stresses have persisted following the early May recoil and even despite a stabilisation in the low $30s, jewellery remains under pressure and this capricious metal is likely to continue to underperform gold in the coming weeks._** - **P** **_latinum became oversold during June and has since been unwinding the fall that took it below $1,700. The passing of the Greek austerity vote was a stimulus and EU developments will be an important driver in the near future._** - **P** **_alladium has also bounced after a sharp fall towards $720, despite fears of further tightening in China. The market remains in deficit, but may struggle to make much more headway in the near term as economic numbers remain mixed and there are nagging concerns about the robustness of the US recovery._** Although prices have picked up from the recent lows the markets are still at risk of dips in price. Sentiment remains cautious among investors and discretionary spending means that “grass roots” demand is mixed. Further downside risks remain, therefore, but we continue to expect a substantial improvement across the sector in the final months of 2011. ##### **Deteriorating economic signals mean that caution remains uppermost** Developments in June and early July have resulted in a substantial “shake-out” in speculative and investment participation in the metals markets and although we expect investment activity to return as we approach year-end, the metals are likely to remain under some pressure in the near term. The price improvements of early July run the risk of being false starts as sentiment is still very cautious at the grass roots level. The time for public and private consolidation is now”. This continues to exceed the government’s targets, despite a series of interest rate rises and increases in bank reserve ratio requirements. After five interest rate hikes in the past nine months (including one on 6th July) and nine increases in reserve requirements over the period, the benchmark one-year lending rate rate now stands at 6.56% and the borrowing rate at 3.50%, while reserve ratios are now generally 21.5%. Real interest rates therefore remain positive, notionally at least, with May headline inflation reported at 5.5%. Food inflation, though, is believed to be much in excess of this figure and regional inflation rates are suspected also to be higher; this is one of the keys driving local gold investment, although core inflation is below 3%. As well as this, there are fears that the Chinese economy may be about to contract. Most observers would welcome such a development with respect to the longer term as it potentially signals a manageable landing, but nervous markets took a degree of fright in June when the Chinese Purchasing Managers’ Index was reported. The index for June fell to 50.9 from 52.0 in May, the lowest reading since February 2009. Some smaller and medium-size companies are reported to be under a degree of stress, and warning of bankruptcies, as a result of the inability to secure bank financing and these developments rekindled fears over the prospect for sustained raw material imports on the basis of possible reduced demand from manufacturers. **I3** Independent - Informed - International Economic Indicators - July 2011 **~~Precious Metals One Month Relative Performance~~** Precious Metals One Year Relative Performance

##### **Professional investors retreat while physical demand is mixed; there is still the potential for further short term weakness** The balance of interest shifted in the gold market during June. We noted in our previous _One Year Forecast_ that the price rebound in the second half of May reflected both physical and professional investor interest, with the latter augmented by further bullish sentiment after the price had pushed through $1,500. Conditions were variable during June and an unsettled market responded sensitively to a range of external developments, both positive and negative. By the end of the month gold had slid below $1,500 and in early July conditions are still nervous. The price continued to rise at the beginning of June, posting a high fix of $1,549.00 in the afternoon of the 6th. Investor interest had started to slow by this stage and the market did not have the momentum to pierce resistance at $1,550. After a correction towards $1,510 in mid-month fresh buying developed in response not just to the drop in price, but also to the release of Chinese and Indian inflation figures that were again higher than the market expected, along with a warning from Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke that a failure to raise the United States debt limit could precipitate a crisis. The problems in the Eurozone remained supportive as the market continued to fret not only over the resolution or otherwise of the Greek position, but also over the continued potential for further contagion. |**~~Gold Supply-Demand & Price Foreca~~**

The longer term bullish elements remain in place, notably the potential impact of bloated balance sheets (especially if, as seems likely, Congress does eventually allow the US’ debt limit to be raised again) and the risk to fiat currencies, notably the euro. To this end it is of interest that gold has been trading sideways in Swiss franc terms since January in a range of just 8% and with a net loss of 4% in price over the period. In dollar terms, by contrast, the range has been 18% with a net price gain of 8%. The implication is that both gold and the Swiss franc are still commanding attention as safe havens, while the dollar has lost favour. For the shorter term, the gold price is as equally disposed to dipping on bearish news as it is

to rallying on bullish developments. We cannot rule out the possibility of a slip to the mid $1,400-$1,500 range in August before the market stabilises and prepares for renewed strength in the final quarter driven both by professional investment and an intensifying of physical purchases at the “grass roots” level. ##### **Physical demand; varying within regions** The physical market is fluid. Consumers in some areas have been returning to the market as heavy buyers into price dips, while other countries have been experiencing physical sales into price strength; others appear to be adopting a “wait and see” attitude. In China, where the reported local annualised inflation rate for May was 5.5% (see page I3 for more discussion of the Chinese economy), gold demand has remained robust although there were signs of a slight dwindling of interest as gold prices rose in the first half of June. Turnover in the physical gold contracts on the Shanghai Gold Exchange averaged 4.8 tonnes in the first three weeks of June as gold approached $1,550; volumes jumped as prices fell, however, and averaged 6.2 tonnes per day over the rest of June and into early July, a jump of 30%. The average daily turnover on the Exchange in the first half of 2011 was 8.0 tonnes. Investors are still concerned about domestic inflationary forces, and demand for investment bars remains strong. In India, demand for bullion has been robust and has been exerting a relatively heavy call on the international market. Jewellery, though, is more variable, reflecting a widespread international trend over recent months in

favour of bullion bars at the expense of jewellery with its higher (fabrication) charges. In early July, however, traders have been reporting a return of jewellery interest in the wake of the sharp falls in price and are of the view that some merchants may start restocking in the coming weeks. The fall in dollar prices through $1,500 in late June led to a drop through Rp22,000 per ten kg, where there had previously been solid price support and this has generated fresh buying activity. For the longer term, there has been some concern expressed locally about the prospects for this year’s harvest because the monsoon rains are forecast to be below normal. The long-term forecast is for this year’s rainfall to be 95% of the long-term average - although this carries a tolerance of 4% either way. The government has, however, said that it is targeting a 245Mt grain harvest in the 2011-2012 season, which would be a record high and rains have been normal so far. Healthy demand in India and China is in contrast to parts of the Middle East, where activity is generally sluggish. Some merchants have been building inventory when prices have dipped, while others have been returning slow-moving stock for recycling and in Saudi Arabia in particular the trend towards lighter pieces has been sustained (traditionally Saudi jewellery has been 21-carat, usually heavy pieces with quite chunky designs). In the Far East, conditions are mixed. There have been some pockets of buying into price weakness, but equally there have been bouts of resale into price strength.
